items.x_text:
FEC hacking attempt: the US election finance regulator took web services offline over 'a bad actor attempting to breach FEC systems', per an email seen by Reuters. E-filing is down a week before the midterms. No breach confirmed.

#ElectionSecurity #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
A week before the midterms, the FEC's filing system went dark. 🗳️

What Reuters reported (27 Oct):
→ An FEC e-filings officer emailed compliance firms: "We have a bad actor attempting to breach FEC systems"
→ The FEC took its web-facing services offline; e-filing has been down since about 10 p.m. ET on Monday 26 Oct
→ 24-hour and 48-hour spending reports can't be filed; past reports are still searchable
→ No breach or data loss has been confirmed, and attackers haven't been named
→ The FEC doesn't run elections, so it says voting shouldn't be affected. The midterms are on 3 Nov

Why it matters: a defensive shutdown can stop an intrusion and still stop the business. Know your manual fallback for deadline-bound filings before you need it.

items.send_to: anyone you know on So-net or Docomo

cover.hook: 2,585,481 customer records. One ISP member database.
cover.sub: Sony Network Communications says an unauthorized party got into its So-net member database. Docomo Hikari users are hit too.

slides.title: Four days to notice
slides.body: The breach happened on 19 October and was detected on 23 October. Sony announced it on 27 October, shut down the compromised servers and blocked external communication.

slides.label: records exposed
slides.note: 2,141,986 So-net + 443,495 plala (S Course) records used for Docomo Hikari

slides.title: What was taken
slides.body: Names, phone numbers, email addresses, user IDs, dates of birth, gender and internet connection IDs. For 54,401 email accounts, passwords were exposed too. Sony says no banking or card details were exposed.

slides.title: Phishing comes next
slides.body: NTT Docomo is warning of phishing emails and fake sites impersonating its d POINT Club and a Universal Studios Japan campaign. Neither company had confirmed misuse of the data as of 27 October.

slides.title: What to do
items: Change your So-net / plala email password
Change it anywhere you reused it
Watch for SMS and calls using your details

items.question: How fast would you spot an intruder in your customer database?
items.x_text:
Sony Network Communications / So-net breach: 2,585,481 customer records exposed, including 443,495 used for NTT Docomo Hikari. Names, phone numbers, birth dates and, for 54,401 email accounts, passwords. Detected 4 days after the break-in.

#DataBreach #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
2.58 million ISP customer records. Found 4 days after the break-in. 🔓

What Sony Network Communications disclosed (via BleepingComputer, 28 Oct):
→ An unauthorized party accessed the So-net member database on 19 Oct; it was detected on 23 Oct
→ 2,585,481 records: 2,141,986 So-net and 443,495 plala (S Course), which serves NTT Docomo's Docomo Hikari
→ Exposed: names, phone numbers, email addresses, user IDs, dates of birth, gender, internet connection IDs
→ 54,401 email accounts had their passwords exposed; Sony says no banking or card details were
→ Docomo warns of phishing posing as d POINT Club and a Universal Studios Japan campaign

What to do: change the password, and anywhere it was reused. Treat 'reward' emails and texts with suspicion.

items.x_text:
Volt Typhoon 'Silent Train': Lumen's Black Lotus Labs says the China-linked group used at least 4 zero-days, incl. VeloCloud Orchestrator, Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN and N-able N-central, relaying through hacked routers in sessions under 8 hours.

#ZeroDay #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
Four zero-days. In and out in under 8 hours. 🚆

What Lumen's Black Lotus Labs reported (via BleepingComputer, 28 Oct):
→ It attributes 'Silent Train', a relay framework of rotating hacked routers and VPS, to China's Volt Typhoon
→ At least four zero-days exploited, incl. VeloCloud Orchestrator (CVE-2026-16812), Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN (CVE-2026-20127) and N-able N-central (CVE-2025-8875, CVE-2025-8876)
→ Sessions typically end within 8 hours, then tooling, keys and configs are wiped
→ Some hacked enterprise systems were kept for 1 to 3 months
→ Targets include telecoms, government, defence, utilities, MSPs and emergency services

What to do this week: patch management platforms first, take admin interfaces off the internet, centralise logs with longer retention and watch for unusual admin activity.

items.send_to: whoever runs your public feedback forms

cover.hook: 3 in 4 responses to a UK government consultation came from bots.
cover.sub: 90,835 of 118,756 responses on disposable vapes were flagged as fraudulent, per a new Tobacco Control study.

slides.label: of responses were bot-generated
slides.note: 90,835 of 118,756 responses to the 2023 UK consultation

slides.title: All aimed at one question
slides.body: Every bot response targeted a single multiple-choice question, opposing restrictions on disposable vape sales. The researchers call it the first documented large-scale automated interference in a formal public health consultation.

slides.title: It flipped the result
slides.body: With the bots removed, 77% of valid respondents supported restrictions: the opposite of what the raw data showed. The Department of Health and Social Care flagged the responses with bot detection.

slides.title: Who did it? Unknown
slides.body: The researchers say the source and sponsor can't be determined. They note the scale and consistency suggest a coordinated campaign, but attribute it to no one.

slides.title: If you run public input
items: Add bot detection to every public form
Check for identical answers at scale

items.question: Would your feedback forms notice 90,000 fake answers?
items.x_text:
UK vapes consultation: 90,835 of 118,756 responses (76%) were bot-generated, per a Tobacco Control study. All targeted one question. With bots removed, 77% backed restrictions: the opposite result. Source unknown.

#AIThreats #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
3 in 4 responses to a UK government consultation came from bots. 🤖

What a new Tobacco Control study found (BMJ Group, 27 Oct):
→ 90,835 of 118,756 responses (76%) to the 2023 UK consultation on disposable vapes were flagged as fraudulent by the health department's bot detection
→ Every one targeted a single multiple-choice question opposing restrictions on disposable vape sales
→ With the bots removed, 77% of valid respondents supported restrictions: the opposite of the raw result
→ The researchers say the source and sponsor can't be determined
→ They call it the first documented large-scale automated interference in a formal public health consultation

Why it matters: any public input channel, from consultations to reviews to surveys, can be flooded. Detect bots, look for identical answers at scale, and publish how you filter.

#Ransomware #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
Police now hold data on 3,000+ customers of a crime host. 🚨

What happened (via BleepingComputer, 28 Oct):
→ The FBI seized the domain of Virtualine, a 'bulletproof' host sold on cybercrime forums that promised to shield customers from complaints and police
→ Dutch police seized dozens of servers in Limburg, taking hundreds of virtual servers offline, and recovered data on 3,000+ customers
→ Germany's Hessen police and the UK's NCA took part, with OverRIPE and Lumen
→ Chainalysis linked its Bitcoin payment addresses to ransomware operators; TRM puts ransomware at about 5% of its flows
→ It also traded as Secury, Massgod, Spamhouse, Lanedo and Omegatech, and is still partly online

What to do: add Virtualine's network ranges to your blocklists and hunt for past connections to them.
